<reason>Both sides were polished and honest, but CON built the stronger path. PRO's spine was the honor-vs-memory distinction plus a sharp fork (salute or mere address). CON answered the fork with a coherent middle position — the fossil records past honor without performing present endorsement — and then turned the equivocation charge back on PRO: A drained the honor to dodge the audit costs and revived it to claim harm, leaving its injury partly circular. On the other decisive axis, PRO's only answer to the purge/audit objection was the word "primarily," and CON's sustained textual attack (the motion condemns honoring slaveholders, and the capital honors one; "founder dominates slaveholder" is a verdict, not a rule; Columbus already splits constituencies) was never met with an administrable standard — A asserted "the floor is in the sentence" but never wrote the rule. CON's closing crystallized two clean voting issues (no floor, non-repeal ≠ endorsement). Minor dings for CON: the clipped opening and the inaccurate "not in the motion" flourish, though the substance stood.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's turn of PRO's central dilemma (B2.1/B2.6, sealed in B4.2): the name "records the honor, it does not perform it," and PRO "cannot drain the honor when answering costs and revive it when claiming harms" — converting A's best weapon into a self-contradiction charge while keeping the Washington/"primarily" pressure that A never escaped.</best_rebuttal>
